overview: This unit covers propositions (Aussagen) with truth values 0 and 1, their operators, and the laws of Boolean algebra (Boolesche Algebra). Set operations illustrate the same structure; truth tables (Wahrheitstabellen) and justified transformations establish equalities. Functional completeness (funktionale Vollständigkeit) describes which operators can express every Boolean function, while duality (Dualität) derives further valid equations from valid ones.

entries.short: A proposition is a sentence with exactly one truth value: 0 or 1.
entries.explanation: A proposition (Aussage) is a declarative sentence whose truth or falsity is unambiguous. In Boolean algebra, 1 represents true and 0 represents false. A phrase such as “Fred’s sister” is not a proposition because it has no truth value that can be checked.
entries.example: “10 is even” has truth value 1; “9 is prime” has truth value 0.
pitfalls: Questions and incomplete phrases do not automatically have a truth value.
entries.heading: 1 · Grundlagen und logische Operatoren

entries.short: Logical operators combine propositions or invert their truth values.
entries.explanation: Negation ¬a is 1 when a=0; conjunction a∧b is 1 when both inputs are 1, and inclusive disjunction a∨b is 1 when at least one input is 1. Equivalence a↔b is 1 when both inputs are equal; exclusive disjunction a⊕b is 1 when exactly one input is 1. Implication a→b is 0 only when a=1 and b=0.
entries.example: For a=1 and b=0, a∧b=0, a∨b=1, a⊕b=1, and a↔b=0.
pitfalls: Logical OR is inclusive and yields 1 even when both inputs are true.
Equivalence and exclusive disjunction have opposite truth values.
entries.heading: 1 · Grundlagen und logische Operatoren

entries.short: The implication a→b is false exactly when a=1 and b=0.
entries.explanation: The proposition a→b is read as “if a, then b.” It is true when a is false or b is true; it is false only when a true premise has a false conclusion. It specifies a truth condition and does not, by itself, assert a cause-and-effect relationship.
entries.example: For a=0 and b=0, a→b=1; for a=1 and b=0, a→b=0.
pitfalls: Implication is not the same as inclusive OR a∨b.
entries.heading: 1 · Grundlagen und logische Operatoren

entries.short: The plus sign can denote Boolean OR, for which 1+1=1.
entries.explanation: In the lecture notation, ∨ and + can both denote Boolean OR; correspondingly, ∧ can be written as ·. We have 1+1=1 because OR is true whenever at least one operand is 1. Here, the plus sign does not denote ordinary addition.
entries.example: a+b can stand for a∨b; thus 1+1=1.
pitfalls: Boolean addition must not be confused with ordinary addition.
entries.heading: 1 · Grundlagen und logische Operatoren

entries.short: Operator precedence and parentheses determine which parts of a logical expression belong together.
entries.explanation: Parentheses make the scope of a connective or negation unambiguous. When constructing a truth table, evaluate the inner subexpressions first and pay particular attention to which entire parenthesized expression a negation bar covers. Write parentheses explicitly whenever the grouping might otherwise be ambiguous.
entries.example: In ¬(a∨c)∧b, the negation applies to the entire disjunction a∨c.
pitfalls: An outer negation bar can cover an entire parenthesized expression, not just its first operand.
entries.heading: 1 · Grundlagen und logische Operatoren

entries.short: Boolean algebra is a system for calculating with the values 0 and 1 using logical operators and their own laws.
entries.explanation: Boolean variables take the values 0 or 1 and are combined using AND, OR, and NOT. These operations obey their own laws, including both distributive laws. The same structure is also called switching algebra when used to describe logic circuits.
entries.example: We have 1∨1=1 and 1∧1=1.
pitfalls: Boolean operations do not always follow the rules of ordinary arithmetic.
entries.heading: 1 · Grundlagen und logische Operatoren

entries.short: Switching algebra refers to the application of Boolean algebra to logic circuits.
entries.explanation: In switching algebra, truth values and Boolean operators describe logical states and how they are combined. It uses the same laws as Boolean algebra. This makes it possible to simplify circuit expressions and check whether they are equal.
entries.example: An AND operation with inputs a and b is represented as a∧b.
pitfalls: Switching algebra uses the Boolean values 0 and 1; the plus sign for OR does not denote ordinary addition.
entries.heading: 1 · Grundlagen und logische Operatoren

entries.short: Boolean operators correspond to set complement, intersection, and union.
entries.explanation: A Boolean variable can represent whether an element belongs to a set. Then ¬a corresponds to the complement Aᶜ, a∧b to the intersection A∩B, and a∨b to the union A∪B. The value 0 corresponds to the empty set ∅ and the value 1 to the universal set U; Venn diagrams illustrate these relationships.
entries.example: a∨(b∧c) corresponds to A∪(B∩C): an element is in A or in both B and C.
pitfalls: The complement depends on the chosen universal set U.
entries.heading: 2 · Zusammenhang zur Mengenlehre und Venn-Diagramme

entries.short: Boolean laws are valid equations that can be used to transform logical expressions.
entries.explanation: The laws include commutativity, associativity, absorption, distributivity, complementation, identity, domination, idempotence, and De Morgan’s laws. Many laws have both an OR form and an AND form, related by duality. In a formal proof, each transformation step is justified by an appropriate law.
entries.example: By idempotence, a∧a=a.
pitfalls: A transformation is not a verifiable proof if the laws used are not identifiable.
entries.heading: 3 · Die Booleschen Gesetze — dein Spickzettel

entries.short: The order of the operands does not affect AND or OR.
entries.explanation: For OR, a∨b=b∨a; for AND, a∧b=b∧a. This law allows the operands to be swapped without changing the expression’s value. It can reorder an expression to make it easier to compare with another expression.
entries.example: b∨a can be transformed into a∨b.
pitfalls: The law swaps operands but does not change their internal expressions.
entries.heading: 3 · Die Booleschen Gesetze — dein Spickzettel

entries.short: With repeated AND or OR, the parentheses can be regrouped.
entries.explanation: For OR, (a∨b)∨c=a∨(b∨c); for AND, (a∧b)∧c=a∧(b∧c). The law changes how repeated instances of the same operator are grouped without changing the order of the operands. It does not allow arbitrary regrouping of different operators.
entries.example: (a∨b)∨c equals a∨(b∨c).
pitfalls: Associativity applies to repeated AND or repeated OR, not to an arbitrary mixture of the two operators.
entries.heading: 3 · Die Booleschen Gesetze — dein Spickzettel

entries.short: In Boolean algebra, both AND over OR and OR over AND are distributive.
entries.explanation: We have a∧(b∨c)=(a∧b)∨(a∧c) and a∨(b∧c)=(a∨b)∧(a∨c). Both forms are valid in Boolean algebra and differ from the familiar distributive law of ordinary arithmetic. The two forms are duals of each other.
entries.example: a∧(b∨c) can be transformed into (a∧b)∨(a∧c).
pitfalls: OR also distributes over AND.
entries.heading: 3.1 Warum ist Distributivität besonders?

entries.short: An operand absorbs a connective in which that same operand appears again.
entries.explanation: The two forms are a∨(a∧b)=a and a∧(a∨b)=a. In both cases, the value of b cannot change the result. The two forms are duals of each other.
entries.example: a∨(a∧b) simplifies to a.
pitfalls: Absorption is not the same as idempotence, because the absorbed part also contains another operand.
entries.heading: 3 · Die Booleschen Gesetze — dein Spickzettel

entries.short: A proposition OR its negation yields 1, and ANDed with its negation yields 0.
entries.explanation: We have a∨¬a=1 and a∧¬a=0. A proposition and its negation cannot both be false, nor can they both be true. The law concerns a variable and its negation.
pitfalls: The complement law concerns a variable and its negation, not two arbitrary variables.
entries.heading: 3 · Die Booleschen Gesetze — dein Spickzettel

entries.short: 0 is the identity element for OR, and 1 is the identity element for AND.
entries.explanation: We have a∨0=a and a∧1=a. The identity element leaves the value of a unchanged. Which value acts as the identity depends on whether OR or AND is used.
entries.example: a∧1 simplifies to a.
pitfalls: The identity element is 0 for OR and 1 for AND.
entries.heading: 3 · Die Booleschen Gesetze — dein Spickzettel

entries.short: OR with 1 yields 1, and AND with 0 yields 0.
entries.explanation: We have a∨1=1 and a∧0=0. In both equations, the constant determines the result regardless of the value of a. The laws are duals of each other.
entries.example: a∨1 yields 1 for both a=0 and a=1.
pitfalls: Under the domination law, the constant determines the result; under the identity law, a remains unchanged.
entries.heading: 3 · Die Booleschen Gesetze — dein Spickzettel

entries.short: Combining a proposition with itself yields the same proposition.
entries.explanation: We have a∨a=a and a∧a=a. Repeated OR or AND with the same truth value adds no new condition. The law applies to both OR and AND.
entries.example: a∨a∨a simplifies to a by repeated application of idempotence.
pitfalls: Idempotence does not hold for arbitrary logical operators.
entries.heading: 3 · Die Booleschen Gesetze — dein Spickzettel

entries.short: Negating a connective negates its operands and swaps AND and OR.
entries.explanation: We have ¬(a∨b)=¬a∧¬b and ¬(a∧b)=¬a∨¬b. Removing the outer negation therefore negates both operands and swaps the operator. These laws help transform and simplify negated expressions.
entries.example: ¬(a∨b) can be written as ¬a∧¬b.
pitfalls: When removing the outer negation, negate the operands and swap the operator.
related: Functional completeness of AND and NOT
entries.heading: 3 · Die Booleschen Gesetze — dein Spickzettel

entries.short: Double negation cancels out, and negation swaps 0 and 1.
entries.explanation: We have ¬0=1, ¬1=0, and ¬(¬a)=a. Double negation is called involution. These rules allow negations to be simplified and constants to be rewritten.
entries.example: ¬(¬a) simplifies to a.
pitfalls: A single negation remains; only two consecutive negations cancel out.
entries.heading: 3 · Die Booleschen Gesetze — dein Spickzettel

entries.short: An algebraic proof derives the target equation through transformations, each justified by a Boolean law.
entries.explanation: Start with one side of the equation and transform it using valid Boolean laws until you reach the other side. Explicitly justify each step by naming the law used. Once you reach the target side, the equality is proved.
entries.example: ¬(¬a∨c)∧b=¬(¬a∨c)∧¬¬b=¬(¬a∨c)∧¬(¬b)=¬((¬a∨c)∨¬b)=¬((¬b∨c)∨¬a); the steps use involution, double-negation notation, De Morgan’s law, associativity, and commutativity.
pitfalls: Skipping several transformations without justification makes a proof difficult to verify.
related: Formal proof of the absorption law
entries.heading: 4.3 Methode B: Umformen mit Axiomen

entries.term: Formal proof of the absorption law
entries.short: The equation a∧(a∨b)=a can be derived through four justified transformations.
entries.explanation: Start with the left-hand side and use the identity law to substitute a∨0 for a. Then apply distributivity, simplify 0∧b using the domination law, and finally remove the identity 0. Justify each step by naming the law that supports it.
entries.example: a∧(a∨b)=(a∨0)∧(a∨b) (identity) = a∨(0∧b) (distributivity) = a∨0 (domination) = a (identity).
pitfalls: The second step uses Boolean distributivity.
entries.heading: 3.2 Absorptionsgesetz formal beweisen (Folien 12–17)

entries.short: A truth table shows the values of a logical expression for every possible input assignment.
entries.explanation: For n binary variables, a complete truth table has exactly 2ⁿ rows, since each variable can independently be 0 or 1. Additional columns record intermediate results and subexpressions so that the final column can be calculated systematically. This makes it possible to compare expressions under the same assignments.
entries.example: For three variables a, b, and c, there are 2³=8 assignments and therefore eight table rows.
pitfalls: An incomplete table is not enough to prove equality for all possible inputs.
entries.heading: 4.2 Methode A: Wahrheitstabelle

entries.short: Two expressions are equal if their final columns agree for every assignment.
entries.explanation: List all assignments of the variables that occur and calculate the necessary subexpressions in separate columns. Then compare the final columns of the two expressions. If they agree in every row, the equality is proved; a row where they differ is a counterexample.
entries.example: For a, b, and c, list the eight assignments, calculate L and R row by row, and compare their final columns.
pitfalls: A single disagreement in the final columns disproves the claimed equality.
Evaluate negation parentheses exactly as they appear in the expression.
entries.heading: 4.2 Methode A: Wahrheitstabelle

entries.short: A Boolean function maps one or more binary inputs to a binary output value.
entries.explanation: A function with n inputs has the form f:{0,1}ⁿ→{0,1}. Exactly one output value is specified for each combination of the n input values. Logical expressions with n variables describe such functions.
entries.example: Conjunction is the function f(a,b)=a∧b.
pitfalls: A Boolean function is determined by its outputs for all input assignments.
entries.heading: 5.1 Was bedeutet das überhaupt?

entries.short: Arity specifies how many inputs an operator or function takes.
entries.explanation: A 0-ary operator is a constant such as 0 or 1; a 1-ary operator takes one input, such as negation ¬a. AND and OR are 2-ary; expressions such as a∧b∧c combine three inputs. The set of k-ary Boolean functions can be written as Mᵏ={g | g:{0,1}ᵏ→{0,1}}, and the set of all arities as M=⋃ₖ₌₀∞Mᵏ.
entries.example: ¬a is 1-ary and a∧b is 2-ary.
pitfalls: Arity counts inputs, not the number of distinct operator symbols in an expression.
entries.heading: 5.1 Was bedeutet das überhaupt?

entries.short: A set of operators is functionally complete if it can represent every Boolean function.
entries.explanation: A set of operators M′ is functionally complete if every function f:{0,1}ⁿ→{0,1} can be represented using variables and only operators from M′. This includes being able to express every possible output rule for binary inputs. A complete standard basis is {0,1,∧,∨,¬}.
entries.example: The set of operators {∧,¬} is functionally complete.
pitfalls: A set is not functionally complete merely because it contains several operators.
related: Functional completeness of AND and NOT
entries.heading: 5.1 Was bedeutet das überhaupt?

entries.term: Functional completeness of AND and NOT
entries.short: AND and NOT suffice to represent constants, OR, and therefore every Boolean function.
entries.explanation: Using AND and NOT, the constants can be formed as 0=a∧¬a and 1=¬(a∧¬a). De Morgan’s law gives a∨b=¬(¬a∧¬b). Thus the operators in the complete standard basis {0,1,∧,∨,¬} can be represented using ∧ and ¬, so {∧,¬} is functionally complete.
entries.example: a∨b can be written without the OR operator as ¬(¬a∧¬b).
pitfalls: To prove functional completeness, it is enough to reconstruct a known complete basis.
entries.heading: 5.2 Warum reichen UND + NICHT?

entries.term: Functional completeness of OR and NOT
entries.short: OR and NOT suffice because AND can be derived from them using De Morgan’s law.
entries.explanation: Using OR and NOT, we obtain a∧b=¬(¬a∨¬b). The constants can also be formed: 1=a∨¬a and 0=¬(a∨¬a). Thus the operators in the complete standard basis can be represented, so {∨,¬} is functionally complete.
entries.example: ¬(¬a∨¬b) equals a∧b.
pitfalls: OR alone is not functionally complete.
related: Functional completeness of AND and NOT
entries.heading: 5.2 Warum reichen UND + NICHT?

entries.short: NAND is an operator that outputs the negation of an AND operation.
entries.explanation: The operator is defined by a↑b:=¬(a∧b) and is also called NOT-AND. It can negate an input, since a↑a=¬a. Also, (a↑b)↑(a↑b)=a∧b; because AND and NOT are functionally complete, NAND alone is functionally complete as well.
entries.example: ¬a can be written using NAND as a↑a.
pitfalls: NAND is not the same as AND, because NAND negates the result of AND.
related: Functional completeness of AND and NOT
entries.heading: 5.3 Ein einziger Operator genügt: NAND!

entries.short: The dual of a valid Boolean equation is also valid.
entries.explanation: To form the dual, swap AND and OR, and swap 0 and 1. Variables, negation symbols, and the parenthesis structure remain unchanged. This makes it possible to derive the dual forms of many valid laws directly.
entries.example: By duality, a∨0=a implies a∧1=a.
pitfalls: Negation symbols are neither removed nor changed when forming the dual.
entries.heading: 6.1 Dualitätsprinzip

entries.short: When forming the dual, swap AND and OR, and swap 0 and 1, while leaving variables, negations, and parentheses unchanged.
entries.explanation: In the entire equation, replace each ∧ with ∨ and each ∨ with ∧. Also replace each 0 with 1 and each 1 with 0. Leave variables, negation symbols, and parentheses unchanged; the dual of a valid equation is also valid.
pitfalls: Do not additionally negate or remove the negation of an operator.
Parentheses remain in the same positions.
entries.heading: 6.2 Beispiel der letzten Folie
